kata.name: Singleton duplicate instance with distinct intrinsic values - the accepted value key passes and check emits nothing while the conventional count test catches it (null result; named missing law)
kata.series_report: docs/ref/pattern-kata-dispositions.md Singleton row (unexpressible: unique element - object identity has no predicate); fixtures/katas/singleton/README.md (pre-registered); beads catherine-r5k.7
kata.series_verdict: pre-registered: two Engine rows whose mode values differ satisfy the accepted key {Engine:[mode]} and both accepted equations, so catherine check emits 0 findings; the conventional arm counts the rows and catches the fault. The cardinality half of the law has no predicate on the surface, so the entry is killed with the missing law named.

expected.detail: Two Engine rows with different modes, one per client; the accepted key {Engine:[mode]} is injective on them, and the accepted equations engine = fallback and engine;mode = seen hold per client, so catherine check emits 0 findings. The conventional arm counts the rows (singleton:engine-duplicate). The fault is a cardinality claim (|rows(Engine)| = 1) with no surface form.

cargo run -q -p catherine-cli -- check fixtures/katas/singleton/duplicate-instance.ct.json --json  # exit 0, findings []

comparison.conventional_baseline: scripted conventional singleton test: exactly one Engine row (count assertion), accessor identity per client, mode coherence; the count assertion is the arm that names this fault

baseline.artifact: prototype/singleton_baseline.py sha256:ff109499c871f2b8361c809daddac175dcac9b805d8227aa938864e8479f5873 (scripted conventional singleton test; executed before the probe arm)

expressibility_gap.invariant: exactly one row of the declared singleton object: |rows(Engine)| = 1 (existence and uniqueness)
expressibility_gap.why: the surface has no cardinality or existence constraint over an object's row set. Path equations compare arrows pointwise on rows that already exist; declarative keys state tuple injectivity (at most one row per equal value tuple) and require a non-empty arrow tuple. Neither can say that a row must exist or that the object has one row, so this two-row instance satisfies every accepted constraint and emits nothing.

discrepancies: The key {Engine:[mode]} is the closest existing surface and is deliberately not the law: it is an injectivity (at most one row per equal value tuple) claim. It passes this instance because the two rows differ in value, and it cannot state that a row must exist. A key with an empty arrow tuple - the only syntactic way to mean at most one row over the object - is refused at parse (recorded as the construction probe in the missing-instance entry).
procedure: 1. The law was named before any fixture: exact cardinality / unique element, |rows(Engine)| = 1 with every access path resolving to that row (fixtures/katas/singleton/README.md).
2. The conventional arm (prototype/singleton_baseline.py, sha256 above) ran first: exactly-one row, accessor resolution and row identity, and mode coherence, over the frozen fault set.
3. The probe arm ran the same fixtures through the real CLI: `catherine check --json`; the construction probe is the same binary refusing an unparseable document.

4. Witnesses were mapped to the pre-registered element vocabulary; unique = executed probe elements minus baseline-identified elements. A key collision and a row count resolve to the same element (the duplicate); a construction rejection is recorded, never counted.
5. Verdict follows the recorded rule: empty unique = killed (parity or null); the cardinality half is recorded in expressibility_gap, never invented as a finding.

6. Verdict: the probe names no element outside the baseline's set, so unique is empty and the entry is killed; the cardinality gap is recorded in expressibility_gap, mirroring the disposition row's `object identity has no predicate`.
